strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically relevant question: the stability of Bradley–Terry rankings on widely used LLM evaluation platforms (Chatbot Arena, MT-Bench) under worst-case removal of a tiny fraction of preference data.

The proposed pipeline is computationally efficient (runtime of minutes on a laptop), practically adoptable, and includes a refitting verification step that guards against false positives from the first-order influence approximation.

The empirical analysis is careful in places: it documents deviations from the actual Chatbot Arena leaderboard computation (tie handling, affine post-processing), analyzes both human- and LLM-as-a-judge data, and provides qualitative inspection of the dropped matches (Table 2, Appendix B).

Interesting secondary findings, e.g., MT-Bench rankings being substantially more robust than Chatbot Arena rankings, and the observation that influential dropped matches almost always involve the affected models.
Code is stated to be publicly available, and the paper is clearly written and well-organized.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The core machinery is a direct application of existing tools (AMIP and influence functions for logistic regression, Broderick et al. 2020; Pregibon 1981; additive one-step Newton from Huang et al. 2024) to the Bradley–Terry model, which the authors themselves note is just a logistic regression with a structured design matrix. Proposition 3.1 is essentially trivial (top-k sets are characterized by pairwise score comparisons).

The headline empirical findings are close to a foregone conclusion. Since the top-2 models differ by a small BT score with a ~55% head-to-head win rate, it is almost deterministic that adversarially dropping the matches in which the top model beats the runner-up will flip the ranking. The paper quantifies 'how few' matches are needed but offers little analysis beyond this expected behavior; the connection to (and contrast with) the vote-rigging results of Min et al. (2025) deserves deeper treatment.

Worst-case (adversarial) dropping sensitivity is conflated with ranking fragility in the discussion. Any ranking can be flipped by adversarially deleting matches favoring one model; the more meaningful questions (e.g., robustness to random deletion, or to deletion of natural quality levels) are not analyzed, so claims about 'generalizability' of rankings are stronger than the evidence.

Incomplete validation of the approximation and greedy search. The method may report a ranking as robust when a non-robust subset exists (false negatives from both the first-order approximation and the greedy closest-pair-first ordering). No experiments validate the method against brute-force search on small instances, and no accuracy guarantees are given.

Limited evaluation scope: only two historical datasets (55k Arena snapshot and MT-Bench with ~3k judgments), with outdated models (GPT-4 variants, Claude-1/2). Findings on these snapshots may not reflect current leaderboards with far larger vote pools; no baseline comparisons (e.g., random-drop sensitivity, existing influence-function variants) are provided.
No uncertainty quantification or statistical treatment of the reported flip thresholds; single point estimates per (dataset, k) pair.

The tie-free analysis deviates from the deployed leaderboard computation, so the claim that 'dropping 0.02% changes the top-ranked model' does not directly apply to the actual Chatbot Arena rankings as published.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant question: the stability of Bradley–Terry rankings used in high-profile platforms like Chatbot Arena and MT-Bench.
The proposed workflow is computationally cheap (top-k robustness on ~50k evaluations in under 3 minutes on a laptop), which makes it plausible as a practical auditing tool.
The refitting/verification step after the AMIP heuristic reduces the risk of false positives from the first-order approximation.
The code is stated to be publicly available, and the paper is generally well organized and easy to follow.
The qualitative analysis of which matches get dropped (Section 4.4, Appendix B) is a nice touch and gives some insight into the mechanism of rank flips.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core machinery is a direct application of the existing AMIP / influence-function data-dropping framework (Broderick et al., 2020; Shiffman et al., 2023) to the Bradley–Terry model. The BT-as-logistic-regression reformulation is standard, and Proposition 3.1 is a triviality (a set that dominates all others by pairwise comparison is the top-k set). The contribution is essentially running a known tool on two public datasets.

The headline finding is arguably expected and close to tautological. When two adjacent models differ by 0.034 BT score with a 55% head-to-head win rate, it is unsurprising that a handful of matchups can flip their order. The paper does not contextualize worst-case sensitivity against a natural baseline (e.g., random-drop bootstrap or jackknife distributions of rank flips), so the reader cannot judge whether 0.02–0.05% flips indicate an alarming fragility or just ordinary sampling noise amplified by a worst-case criterion.

The method does not answer the question practitioners actually care about. Worst-case dropping is a diagnostic, not a threat model (attackers inject votes, as the paper itself notes via Min et al., 2025), and it is not a measure of statistical generalization (random resampling would be). The paper conflates 'worst-case subset can flip ranks' with concerns about 'generalizability and stability' without establishing that link.

Missing validation of the approximation. There is no experiment quantifying how accurately AMIP/one-step-Newton approximates the true worst-case drop effect (e.g., against exact refit-and-search on small synthetic arenas), and no check of false negative rates. Given the greedy early-stopping heuristic (checking only the closest-ranked pairs, justified only anecdotally by Fig. 6), claims that an arena 'is' robust at level α are unsupported — the method can only certify non-robustness, not robustness, yet the paper reports both.

Evaluation is thin: only two historical datasets (Chatbot Arena ~2023–24 snapshot, MT-Bench with 3,335 evaluations), no synthetic simulations where ground truth is known, no other ranking schemes (e.g., Elo with ties, mBT as actually deployed), and conclusions such as 'MT-Bench is more robust due to expert annotators' are speculative confounds (dataset size and score gaps differ drastically across the two benchmarks).

The comparison of human vs. LLM-as-judge sensitivity (Section 4.3) is based on a handful of flips and inconsistent orderings across k (humans more sensitive for k in {5,20}, LLMs for k in {1,3,10}), which does not support a robust 'just as sensitive' conclusion.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence: e.g., the statement that dropped responses 'appear similar in content' rests on manual visual inspection of five examples (Table 2), and the discussion that expert annotation causes robustness is asserted without isolating confounds.

Some presentation issues: the code URL is missing/blank in the text; the top-k robustness definition in Eq. (7) compares sets under different weightings in a way that requires care; and the tie-handling deviation from the deployed leaderboard, while acknowledged, weakens the claim of auditing 'the' Arena rankings.

strengths: Timely and practically relevant question: auditing the stability of Bradley–Terry rankings on widely used platforms (Chatbot Arena, MT-Bench) addresses a real concern for the LLM evaluation community, complementing prior work on vote-rigging (Min et al., 2025) and leaderboard integrity (Singh et al., 2025).

The proposed procedure is computationally lightweight and practical: by casting BT as logistic regression and applying influence-score-based AMIP / additive one-step Newton approximations with a final refit verification, top-k robustness on ~50K evaluations runs in minutes on a laptop; this makes the tool genuinely adoptable by leaderboard maintainers.

Useful diagnostic outputs beyond a binary robust/non-robust answer: the method identifies the specific influential evaluations, enabling qualitative inspection (Section 4.5, Table 2) and the analysis of which players are involved in dropped matches (Section 4.4, Appendix B), which yields interpretable findings.

Empirical comparisons are reasonably multi-faceted: human vs. LLM-as-a-judge judges, Chatbot Arena vs. MT-Bench, and multiple k values, with a sensible observation that expert-annotated MT-Bench is more robust than crowdsourced Arena.
Clear, honest accounting of deviations from the platform's actual computation (tie handling, affine post-processing) in Section 3.1, and code is stated to be publicly released for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core machinery is a direct application of AMIP/influence functions (Broderick et al., 2020; Pregibon, 1981) to BT scores; Proposition 3.1 is a trivial observation about sorted sets. The contribution is largely 'existing robustness auditing applied to a new domain,' which may not meet the novelty bar at a top-tier venue.

Missing a critical baseline: the paper never compares worst-case dropping against random dropping. If a random subset of similar size also flips rankings (plausible given Fig. 6 shows flips occur exactly for near-tied models with tiny win margins), then the 'adversarial sensitivity' framing is overstated and the headline finding (0.02% flips the top rank) may be an artifact of near-identical top models rather than a meaningful fragility result.

No guarantees for the approximate/greedy procedure: AMIP uses a first-order approximation and the top-k check is greedy (closest pairs first, early termination), so a 'robust' verdict does not certify absence of a flipping subset; the paper does not empirically validate the approximation quality (e.g., against exact search on small instances), so claims of the form 'the arena is robust at level α' are unsupported.

Evaluation scope is narrow and dated: only two historical datasets (~57K and ~3.3K evaluations) with models from the GPT-4-0125 era; no experiments on more recent or larger-scale arena data, other ranking models (e.g., Elo variants, tie-aware BT), or other preference benchmarks, limiting generalizability of the conclusions.

Statistical rigor is thin: no confidence intervals or uncertainty quantification on the reported flip thresholds; single point estimates from an approximate optimization; the claim that dropped responses are 'similar in content' rests on visual inspection of five examples.

Presentation issues: the code URL is blank in the submitted manuscript (Section 1); Figure 2's caption/axis interpretation is potentially confusing (absolute fraction dropped vs. 'percentage'); some results (e.g., win-percent column in Table 1) suggest the flips are predictable near-ties, which is acknowledged but not analyzed as a caveat to the central claim.

strengths: Timely and significant question: assessing the statistical robustness of widely used LLM leaderboard rankings (Chatbot Arena and derivatives) is of clear practical relevance to the AI community, and the paper provides the first systematic method for worst-case data-dropping robustness in BT-based ranking systems.

Methodologically careful design: the AMIP approximation is used only to identify candidate influential subsets, followed by an exact BT refit to verify every reported non-robustness finding. This means reported fragility results (e.g., dropping 2 of 57,477 human preferences flips the Chatbot Arena top model) are definitive witnesses, not approximation artifacts; the paper is honest that false negatives are possible.

Comprehensive and well-rounded empirical evaluation: multiple arenas (Chatbot Arena, Vision, Webdev, Search, MT-bench), human vs. LLM-as-a-judge comparisons, classical BT use cases (NBA, ATP tennis), robustness of bootstrap-CI-based rankings, a uniform-random-dropping control experiment showing worst-case and random deletion probe distinct failure modes, and qualitative inspection of the surfaced influential preferences.

Good positioning and discussion: the paper clearly distinguishes its notion of non-robustness from adversarial vote-rigging and annotator-quality work, discusses the masking/false-negative limitation, ties fragility to narrow BT score margins, and offers actionable recommendations for arena design.
Practical and fast: the method runs on ~50k preferences in minutes on a laptop, lowering adoption barriers for leaderboard maintainers.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core machinery is largely a direct application of existing AMIP/influence-function tools (Broderick et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2025a) to the BT model; the key theoretical result (Proposition B.1) is elementary, and the algorithm is a greedy pairwise check. The contribution is primarily empirical transfer of known statistics methods to a new domain.

The headline finding is arguably foreseeable: with narrow BT score margins at the top of the leaderboard, some small worst-case subset will almost necessarily flip the ranking — the paper itself confirms sensitivity is driven by proximity of scores (Figure 18, Section F.1). The novelty of the empirical conclusion over prior work (Min et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025) is incremental, mainly differing in that votes are removed rather than added or replaced.

Interpretation concerns: worst-case deletion is inherently an adversarial quantity, and the paper's claim that this differs from adversarial attacks because it occurs 'after data collection' and 'without adversarial intent' may understate the interpretive ambiguity — the check largely diagnoses narrow margins/low separability rather than a distinct statistical pathology, and a rigorous robustness guarantee (i.e., proving robustness) is not achievable with this method due to false negatives.
Reproducibility could be stronger: while datasets are public, no explicit code release is stated in the manuscript.

Presentation issues: minor inconsistencies (e.g., '0.003%' vs. '0.0003%' in Related Work), typos (e.g., 'that sharpens distinctions', 'amd'), and the qualitative analysis relies on a single LLM judge (GPT-5.1) without human validation, weakening Section 4.4's conclusions about 'atypical' preferences.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant question: the statistical robustness of widely used LLM leaderboards (Chatbot Arena, MT-bench, etc.), with direct practical significance for model developers and benchmark users.

The proposed pipeline is well-executed methodologically: the AMIP approximation is used only to nominate candidate subsets, and all non-robustness claims are verified by exact refitting of the BT model, which avoids false positives; the authors are also transparent that false negatives are possible and discuss masking effects honestly (Section H).

The empirical evaluation has good breadth: five LLM arenas (human and LLM-as-a-judge variants), two sports datasets as classical BT use cases, multiple k values, bootstrap-CI-based rankings, and a uniform-vs-worst-case data-dropping contrast (Table 3) that clearly distinguishes the two failure modes.

The runtime analysis (under 3 minutes on a laptop for ~50k evaluations) and the ability to surface the specific prompt–response pairs driving ranking flips make the tool practically adoptable by leaderboard maintainers.

The derived recommendations (richer feedback signals, more discriminative prompts, higher-quality annotation) are sensible and grounded in the analysis, e.g., the MT-bench vs. crowdsourced-arena comparison.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core machinery is a direct application of existing tools: AMIP/influence functions (Broderick et al., 2020), BT-as-logistic-regression (standard), and a straightforward greedy pairwise search. The adaptation to BT rankings is incremental, and the reduction of top-k robustness to pairwise checks (Prop. B.1) is elementary. The main contribution is empirical rather than methodological.

The headline claim is somewhat inflated relative to its significance. Dropping 2 of 57k votes flips GPT-4-0125-preview and GPT-4-1106-preview, but these two models have nearly identical BT scores (1250.5 vs 1249.97) and heavily overlapping bootstrap intervals. Flipping the ordering of two statistically indistinguishable models is expected behavior for any estimator, not a shocking fragility. Although the paper analyzes bootstrap-based rankings (A.1), the abstract and title lead with the most sensational framing, which overstates the practical implication that leaderboards are 'untrustworthy.'

The central negative result is somewhat predictable: given close score margins at the top of any arena, a worst-case targeted deletion will flip adjacent ranks. The paper's own Figure 18 confirms robustness is essentially a function of BT score gaps, so the finding amounts to 'when scores are close, rankings are close'—a result whose main content was already anticipated by Zhao et al. (2025) and the vote-rigging literature.

The MT-bench robustness finding is confounded: MT-bench has only six models and 80 prompts, so higher robustness may reflect fewer models, fewer comparisons, or dataset size rather than 'expert annotators and carefully constructed prompts' as the paper speculates.

The qualitative analysis of dropped preferences relies on a single LLM judge (GPT-5.1) accessed through a chat interface in two examples—an anecdotal and weakly reproducible methodology for the claim that influential preferences are 'atypical.'

Presentation issues undermine polish: a numerical inconsistency in the headline number (0.003% in the abstract vs. 0.0003% in Section 5.1), an evident duplicate/near-verbatim repetition of the same paragraphs in Appendix E, typos ('amd', '22st place', 'a tile'), and no clear statement about releasing code, which limits reproducibility of the greedy algorithm's specific choices (pair ordering, tie handling, approximation variant).

The utility of the method as a 'robustness check' is limited by its one-sidedness: it can only certify non-robustness, never robustness (Section H), yet the paper's Table 1 implicitly presents robustness orderings of arenas, which the false-negative caveat does not fully support.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: assessing statistical robustness of BT-based LLM leaderboard rankings to worst-case data-dropping, which is complementary to existing adversarial-attack analyses (vote rigging, judge gaming) and to prior case studies (Zhao et al., 2025).

Technically sound methodology: the reduction of top-k robustness to pairwise score robustness is correct, the AMIP approximation is used appropriately for candidate-subset identification, and—crucially—every reported non-robustness is verified by exact refitting, so all reported flips are definitive (no false positives).
Efficient and practical: runs on ~50k evaluations in under 3 minutes on a laptop, making the check genuinely adoptable by leaderboard operators; explicit runtime and computational cost analysis.

Broad empirical evaluation: five LLM arenas (Chatbot, Vision, Webdev, Search, MT-bench), human vs. LLM-judge variants, plus NBA/ATP baselines; multiple k values; bootstrap-CI-based rankings also analyzed, showing fragility persists even accounting for sampling uncertainty.

Useful supporting analyses: uniform vs. worst-case dropping comparison (Table 3) showing they probe distinct failure modes; sensitivity-vs-score-margin analysis; qualitative inspection showing surfaced preferences are atypical/outlier annotations; honest treatment of false negatives due to masking effects (Section H).
Well-written and well-organized, with detailed derivations in the appendix and clear positioning against related work.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core technique is a direct adaptation of AMIP (Broderick et al., 2020) plus a straightforward Proposition (B.1) that top-k sets are characterized by pairwise comparisons; the theoretical contribution is thin.

Some headline findings are relatively unsurprising: fragility of point-estimate rankings when top BT scores are nearly tied is partially a consequence of the method design; the paper's own analysis (Section F.1, Figure 18) confirms sensitivity is driven by narrow score margins, which could invite the critique that the surprising 0.003% figure largely reflects near-ties rather than a deep flaw.

Greedy pair ordering and first-order approximation mean the algorithm can miss non-robustness (false negatives); the 'robust' determinations (e.g., MT-bench at α=1%) are therefore only 'not found to be fragile', which somewhat weakens the contrast claims between arenas.

No comparison against alternative influence-subset methods (e.g., Additive one-step Newton results are described but not systematically reported in the main results), and no release statement of code/data pipeline is explicitly confirmed in the manuscript.

The human vs. LLM-as-a-judge comparison is inconclusive by the authors' own admission, and the qualitative analysis relies on a single LLM judge (GPT-5.1), which is a small sample for supporting the 'outlier preference' interpretation.
